notes: Wikipedia titles this event 'Battle of Utica (203 BC)'; it is the night assault on the reed-and-timber winter camps of Hasdrubal Gisco (Carthage) and Syphax (Numidia) outside the separate, much longer Siege of Utica -- not the siege itself, which never took the city and is excluded here for having no attached battle-outcome or casualty figures of its own. opponent_general_id is left blank because command was genuinely split between two co-equal allied kings/generals of two separate national contingents (Carthage and Numidia), not a single identifiable commander, the same reasoning used for Petelia's blank field elsewhere in this dataset. own_troop_strength (27,500) is the midpoint of modern historians' 25,000-30,000 estimate for Scipio's four reinforced legions; enemy_troop_strength (47,500) uses Hoyos's modern combined estimate over the ancient sources' combined ~93,000 (33,000 Carthaginian + 60,000 Numidian), which modern historians call infeasibly large, the same modern-over-ancient-extreme treatment as Ilipa. enemy_casualties uses the lower end of the ancient range (30,000 killed, Polybius, plus 2,400 captured, the lower of two captured figures given) rather than the higher 40,000-killed/5,000-captured variant, since even the lower figure is flagged by modern historians as likely still inflated and no revised modern total exists in the literature -- same 'use the more conservative reported figure, flag it' precedent as Trasimene/Cannae. own_casualties has no figure beyond 'practically no loss to the Romans' and is a flagged order-of-magnitude placeholder. political_constraint_flag=true: Scipio's African expedition was fought over the objections of Fabius Maximus's Senate faction, with an army built mainly from volunteers and the politically stigmatized 'Cannae legions' (survivors of the 216 BC disaster, serving a punitive posting in Sicily) rather than a fresh state-backed force, reflected in resource_backing_tier=2.

source_citation: Polybius, Histories XV.9-14; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita XXX.32-35; Appian, Punica VII.40-48; Wikipedia 'Battle of Zama' (citing Goldsworthy, Lazenby)
notes: The war-deciding battle; figures here are the mirror of the existing hannibal-zama-202bc row (own/enemy troop strength and casualties swapped) so the two rows agree on the same battle -- own_troop_strength=30,000 (Masinissa's Numidian cavalry, decisive on the day, included), enemy_troop_strength=40,000 (Polybius's figure for Hannibal's mixed veteran/newly-raised force, preferred over Appian's 50,000 per the reasoning already in Hannibal's row), own_casualties=1,500 killed (Goldsworthy: 'a substantial loss for a victorious army, testimony to the hard fighting'), enemy_casualties=40,000 (Polybius's 20,000 killed plus 20,000 captured, essentially Hannibal's entire army). political_constraint_flag=true from Scipio's side too, independent of Hannibal's: the African expedition was launched over Fabius Maximus's Senate opposition with the stigmatized Cannae-legion volunteers (see the Battle of the Camps row's notes), and the pre-battle armistice Scipio had negotiated with Carthage collapsed when a Carthaginian mob seized a storm-driven Roman supply fleet, restarting the war on the eve of the battle. resource_backing_tier=2, one tier below Hannibal's own tier=3 for the same battle -- Hannibal fought on home soil with a hastily but freely mobilized Carthaginian levy, while Scipio's army was still the same under-resourced, politically constrained expeditionary force fielded since 204 BC, a real asymmetry each general's own row records independently rather than forcing to match.

source_citation: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Georgian Chronicles); Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of Armenia; Timothy May, The Mongol Art of War; Wikipedia 'Battle of Khunan'
notes: Co-commanded with Jebe as joint primary decision-makers on an independent reconnaissance-in-force Genghis Khan authorized after the Khwarazmian pursuit reached the Caspian -- same 'co-equal senior partner' standard already documented for Jebe/Subutai jointly in this dataset's Genghis Khan rows is extended here to Subutai's own roster, since no source subordinates either man to the other for this campaign. Troop strength (30,000 Mongols and allies vs. 30,000 Georgian-Armenian coalition) is the figure given for the battle itself; the campaign opened with smaller forces (20,000 Mongol / 10,000 Georgian) that both grew before the decisive engagement. Casualties are only described qualitatively in every source found ('moderate' Mongol, 'heavy' Georgian) -- own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude placeholders consistent with that language, not source-given counts, the same treatment given to several Genghis Khan/Saladin rows elsewhere in this dataset. Feigned-retreat envelopment tactic (classic Jebe/Subutai playbook, also used at Kalka the following year). King George IV of Georgia was mortally wounded in the chest and died of the wound on 18 January 1223; recorded as opponent_general_id as the coalition's named royal commander (atabeg Ivane Mkhargrdzeli also present but not senior to the king).

source_citation: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh; Kirakos Gandzaketsi, History of Armenia; Timothy May, The Mongol Art of War; Wikipedia 'Battle of Khankala (1222)'
notes: Fought weeks/months after Khunan in the same 1222 North Caucasus campaign, same Jebe/Subutai joint-primary command as that row. Opposing coalition (North Caucasians -- Alans, Durdzuk/Vainakh, Circassians, Lekia -- plus Kipchak Turks) was won over by first bribing the Kipchak contingent to abandon the field, then destroying the remainder; Durdzuk forces broke out and escaped the encirclement, the one incomplete part of an otherwise total victory. own_troop_strength uses 25,000 as a round mid-estimate for the infobox's 'fewer than 30,000'; enemy_troop_strength (~50,000) is the coalition figure before the Kipchak defection thinned it. No source gives a specific casualty count for either side -- only 'moderate' Mongol losses against a coalition 'almost entirely wiped out,' with captured survivors reportedly executed; own_casualties and enemy_casualties are order-of-magnitude placeholders on that qualitative language, same treatment as the Khunan row. Two coalition leaders are named ('Yuri', a Cuman/Kipchak chief, wounded; 'Daniel') with no clear single supreme commander identifiable across a multi-ethnic coalition, so opponent_general_id is left blank, the same convention used for Genghis Khan's Zhongxing/Yehuling rows elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Novgorod First Chronicle; Galician-Volhynian Chronicle; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Kalka River'
notes: The best-attested Jebe/Subutai joint-command battle in the sources, and the culmination of the same reconnaissance-in-force campaign as Khunan/Khankala -- treated here as the anchor battle of Subutai's roster. own_troop_strength (23,000) combines the modern-estimated 18,000-20,000 Mongols with their Brodnici (Slavic frontier) allies, who fought alongside them rather than against them. enemy_troop_strength uses 33,000, the midpoint of modern estimates' 20,000-45,000 range for the Rus'-Cuman coalition, rejecting the chronicle claim of up to 80,000 -- same 'prefer the modern historian's corrective over the inflated chronicle figure' precedent already used for Caesar/Genghis/Hannibal elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_casualties (73,000, the midpoint of the commonly cited 70,000-75,000 dead/wounded/captured/missing/deserted/executed figure, 'only every tenth man returned to Rus'') is unusually large relative to even the high end of the troop-strength estimate -- sources reconcile this by folding in the rout and multi-day pursuit slaughter after the battlefield collapse, not battlefield dead alone; flagged here since it is a real feature of the sources, not a data-entry inconsistency. own_casualties ('minor' in every source, no hard figure) is an order-of-magnitude placeholder. Six Rus' princes were killed; Kievan Grand Prince Mstislav III of Kiev, the coalition's senior named commander, was captured and executed (reportedly suffocated under a platform the Mongol commanders then feasted on) -- recorded as opponent_general_id over the more tactically active Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, since Mstislav III held the senior princely title.

source_citation: Rogerius of Apulia, Carmen Miserabile; Yuan Shi; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Battle of Mohi'
notes: Fought under Batu Khan's nominal supreme command of the western campaign, but this is the strongest-documented case in the sources of Subutai as the real tactical author despite a nominally senior prince -- the Yuan Shi states outright 'everything achieved then was due to Subutai's merit,' and the post-battle political dispute (Guyuk and Buri accusing Batu of riding Subutai's coattails to victory) directly names Subutai's role over Batu's, a more direct textual basis than exists for several other Batu-era candidate battles researched and dropped from this roster (see generals.csv note). political_constraint_flag=true for this reason: Subutai held real tactical authority but only nominal subordinate rank beneath a Chinggisid prince, a genuine, well-documented constraint on his formal command authority, not merely normal chain-of-command hierarchy. own_troop_strength (30,000) follows Sverdrup's estimate of 'at least 30,000' engaged, toward the high end of the wide 15,000-30,000 contemporary-source range; enemy_troop_strength (25,000) follows the modern-favored estimate over Juvaini's chronicle claim of roughly double the Mongol force, same inflated-chronicle rejection as the Kalka River row. enemy_casualties (10,000) is the contemporary-source figure (the Western European Epternacher Notiz); later secondary summaries citing up to 40,000-80,000 likely conflate battlefield/pursuit losses with the subsequent countrywide devastation of Hungary, so the more conservative contemporary figure is used. own_casualties has no reliable consensus in any source ('several hundred to several thousand') -- 1,500 is an order-of-magnitude placeholder, not a source-given count; Carpini later reported seeing a large Mongol war-dead cemetery from the campaign in Russia, confirming real but unquantified losses. Effectively ended organized Hungarian resistance for the rest of the year. resource_backing_tier=4, one step above the Caucasus-campaign rows: this is the main western campaign under the reigning Great Khan Ogedei's authorization with the empire's full mobilization behind it, versus the earlier rows' cut-off reconnaissance-in-force.

source_citation: Yuan Shi; Jin Shi; Richard Gabriel, Subotai the Valiant; Wikipedia 'Siege of Kaifeng (1232)'
notes: Ogedei sent two armies to converge on the Jin capital, one under his own nominal command and one under his brother Tolui; once the two forces joined, command passed to Subutai, who led the siege throughout, becoming sole commander for its final phase after Tolui fell ill and died and Ogedei withdrew -- an unambiguous personal-command case, unlike the nearby Battle of Sanfengshan (Feb 1232, the field battle that preceded this siege and destroyed the Jin's last army), which this roster excludes: Wikipedia's own battle-specific article credits Tolui as the tactical planner with Subutai unmentioned, while other sources credit Subutai -- a genuine, unresolved command-attribution split (documented in generals.csv) that this dataset's personal-command bar treats as excludable, the same standard already applied to Zhukov's Stavka-coordinator battles elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_troop_strength (300,000, commonly cited as the Jin defense force: ~120,000 regulars, ~100,000 irregulars, ~80,000-100,000 auxiliaries) is very likely inflated by garrison/auxiliary padding the way several other sieges in this dataset are (cf. Genghis's Yehuling/Zhongxing rows), but no specific modern recount was found to correct it against, so the commonly cited total is used rather than an unsourced guess. enemy_casualties (150,000) is a deliberate downward correction from the commonly repeated 'approximately 95% of the defense force' (~285,000) claim, which implies near-total destruction of an already-inflated force estimate -- the same skepticism already applied to Juvaini's Samarkand death toll in Genghis Khan's roster. Separately, and explicitly excluded from this row's casualties fields since the schema defines them as military losses: an estimated 40-50% of the city's roughly one-million civilian population died from the siege, subsequent famine, and a documented plague outbreak during the 1233 truce negotiations -- a real, separately attested demographic catastrophe, not folded into enemy_casualties here to avoid conflating civilian and military losses. own_casualties (5,000) is an order-of-magnitude placeholder for real but unquantified Mongol losses during the prolonged siege, including the Jin defenders' documented early use of gunpowder 'thunder-crash bomb' weapons (Jin Shi); no source gives a specific Mongol death toll. Jin Emperor Aizong fled the city before its fall (recorded as opponent_general_id, the Jin state's supreme authority throughout the siege) and the city was surrendered by the Han defector general Cui Li rather than stormed; decisiveness=Strategic rather than Rout since the siege ended in a political collapse/flight rather than the destruction of a field army, and the Jin dynasty itself did not fall outright until the follow-on Siege of Caizhou in 1234 (outside this campaign and not personally led by Subutai as far as this research found).

source_citation: Stephen Turnbull, War in Japan 1467-1615 (Osprey); Shincho Koki (primary chronicle, via secondary translation/summary)
notes: Two-wing battle: Oda Nobunaga's main force (23,000) fought the Azai clan on the right while Tokugawa's own contingent (5,000, own_troop_strength here) fought a distinct Asakura force on the left under Asakura Kagetake, reported at 8,000 (enemy_troop_strength) -- a genuinely separate engagement against a genuinely separate enemy commander, not Tokugawa listed as one of several subordinates inside someone else's unified battle plan (contrast the Nagashino exclusion below), so this clears the personal-command bar used elsewhere in this dataset. Casualties are the weak point: Shincho Koki gives 1,100 Asakura dead specifically (used here as enemy_casualties, the one figure that is genuinely wing-specific rather than a whole-battle total), but no source isolates Tokugawa's own losses from the combined Oda-Tokugawa total of 800 killed -- own_casualties=200 here is an order-of-magnitude estimate scaled to Tokugawa's ~18% share of the combined 28,000-strong allied force, not a source-given figure, flagged the same way as several Genghis/Saladin rows elsewhere in this dataset. decisiveness=Tactical since neither the Azai nor Asakura clan was destroyed by this battle; both fought on for another 3 years.

source_citation: A.L. Sadler, The Maker of Modern Japan: The Life of Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu; Stephen Turnbull, Battles of the Samurai / The Samurai Sourcebook
notes: Tokugawa's own clear personal defeat, own_troop_strength includes a 3,000-strong Oda reinforcement contingent that fought under his command at Hamamatsu, not Oda's own (contrast Anegawa, where the Oda and Tokugawa forces fought as two separate wings under separate command). Sources describe the Tokugawa side as 'almost completely annihilated' rather than giving a precise whole-army count; own_casualties=1,000 follows one secondary estimate found (this reads as Tokugawa's elite retainers/close guard specifically, consistent with the famous episode of Ieyasu fleeing back to Hamamatsu castle with only a handful of men, not a literal ~9% army-wide casualty rate) -- flagged as approximate, not a hard source-given total. enemy_casualties=1,500 is the midpoint of the 500-3,000 range given for Takeda losses; no source narrows this further. decisiveness=Rout per this schema's own convention (own army broke).

source_citation: Stephen Turnbull, Samurai Sourcebook / War in Japan 1467-1615 (general coverage of the Takeda-Tokugawa wars; the specific casualty figures below trace to secondary wiki compilations citing Turnbull rather than a page-checked primary quotation)
notes: Substantively a Tokugawa-directed operation, not a subordinate role in an Oda-led plan: Tokugawa built five encirclement forts through 1580 to isolate the Takeda garrison under Okabe Motonobu, with Oda troops present in a supporting rather than commanding capacity -- the reverse of Nagashino's command structure. Recaptures Takatenjin, which Takeda Katsuyori had held since 1574 (part of the territory lost around the Mikatagahara period), so decisiveness=Strategic. own_casualties=130, enemy_casualties=680 (over half the garrison died of starvation before the final breakout in which the remainder, including Okabe, were killed) per Turnbull-citing secondary sources; flagged Low confidence since this row's sourcing could not be independently verified against a page in Turnbull's own text the way several other rows in this dataset were -- weakest-sourced of Tokugawa's included battles.

source_citation: Stephen Turnbull, War in Japan 1467-1615; George Sansom, A History of Japan 1334-1615 (campaign-level characterization)
notes: One engagement within the larger Komaki-Nagakute campaign (March-November 1584); the broader Komaki standoff itself is excluded from this roster as no source gives a discrete casualty figure for a single pitched battle there (it was a months-long fortified stalemate that ended in negotiated peace, not a climactic clash -- same no-quantifiable-casualties bar used elsewhere in this dataset). At Nagakute specifically, sources are mixed on whether Tokugawa personally led the intercepting vanguard or whether Ii Naomasa/Sakakibara Yasumasa commanded the actual strike while Ieyasu directed from close support -- but he personally force-marched the whole pursuit column overnight, was present on the field, made the decision to intercept and then to disengage before Hideyoshi's main army arrived, and fought entirely with his own troops (no Oda contingent in this column) -- closer to the Grant-style 'personally supreme-directed, present on the field' standard already used elsewhere in this dataset than to Nagashino's subordinate-under-Nobunaga's-plan case, so included. own_troop_strength/enemy_troop_strength are for this specific intercepting engagement, not the wider ~30,000 vs ~100,000 campaign totals -- do not confuse the two. enemy_casualties=2,500 uses the low end of a wide 2,500-10,000 range found (the one figure with a specific 'at least' framing in the sourcing, the rest reads as unreconciled inflation); own_casualties=590 was the one figure with reasonable source agreement. decisiveness=Tactical since the wider campaign still ended in stalemate.

source_citation: Anthony J. Bryant, Sekigahara 1600: The Final Struggle for Power (Osprey); Sekigahara Gunki Taisei; Tokugawa Jikki / Chronicles of Toshogu Shrine
notes: Troop strength is comparatively well-attested (Bryant's Osprey monograph gives 75,000 initial / 88,888 by battle time for the Eastern Army against 120,000 initial / 81,890 by battle time for the Western Army -- the by-battle-time figures are used here, since that is the force actually engaged, not the nominal mobilization total). Casualties, unusually for this dataset, have NO clean modern-historian corrective available: the only English-language modern secondary figure found (Bryant, quoted as writing that 'by the end of the day 40,000 heads had been taken') sits ABOVE the Edo-period chronicle range rather than revising it downward, the reverse of the Caesar/Genghis/Hannibal precedent of preferring a modern corrective under an inflated chronicle figure -- so no such correction was applied here. Primary chronicles disagree substantially: Sekigahara Gunki Taisei gives Western Army 8,000-32,000 / Eastern Army 4,000-10,000 killed; Tokugawa Jikki and the Chronicles of Toshogu Shrine give a flat 35,270 Western / 8,000 Eastern. Figures used here (enemy_casualties=20,000, own_casualties=6,000) are chosen as defensible midpoints of the Gunki Taisei range, below the Tokugawa Jikki maximalist figures -- a documented judgment call under genuine unresolved source disagreement, not a resolved consensus number; flagged here so it isn't mistaken for one. source_confidence=Medium rather than Low because troop strength (the input that matters most for OAR/force-ratio metrics) is unusually solid for this battle even though casualties are not. decisiveness=Strategic: ended the succession war and cemented Tokugawa supremacy, though the Western Army was broken largely by mass defection (Kobayakawa Hideaki et al.) rather than destroyed outright in the field, so Rout was not used.

battle_name: Battle of Tennoji (Summer Siege of Osaka)
source_citation: Stephen Turnbull, Osaka 1615: The Last Battle of the Samurai (Osprey)
notes: Climactic field battle of the Summer Campaign of the Siege of Osaka; the earlier Winter Campaign (Nov 1614-Jan 1615) is excluded from this roster despite clear troop strength figures (164,000 vs 120,000) because no source found gives a quantifiable casualty figure for the campaign as a whole -- only qualitative accounts of specific actions like the 4 December repulse at the Sanada-maru redoubt ('severe casualties', no number), the same no-fabrication bar used throughout this dataset. Command note: Tokugawa Hidetada was the sitting shogun and nominal army commander for the Summer Campaign, with Ieyasu formally retired as Ogosho, but sources describe Ieyasu personally directing overall strategy and meeting with Hidetada immediately before the campaign's climax -- credited to Ieyasu here as the real strategic/operational supreme commander despite the formal retirement, the mirror image of Subutai's Mohi row elsewhere in this dataset (there, nominal subordinate rank with real tactical authority; here, nominal retirement with real supreme authority) -- political_constraint_flag=true for this same reason, a genuine tension in formal command authority, not ordinary chain-of-command hierarchy. opponent_general_id names Sanada Yukimura (killed in this battle) as the actual field commander of the Toyotomi defense rather than the nominal Toyotomi Hideyori, same convention used for Subutai's Kaifeng/Mohi rows. Toyotomi casualties of 15,000-18,600 (nearly 50% of the engaged force) and the destruction of the Toyotomi clan itself within days justify decisiveness=Rout, arguably Ieyasu's second most consequential victory after Sekigahara.

source_citation: Fred Anderson, 'Crucible of War' (2000), pp. 34, 53-55; Edward Lengel, 'General George Washington: A Military Life'; William Fowler; Wikipedia 'Battle of Jumonville Glen' cross-checked for the disputed troop-strength breakdown
notes: own_troop_strength (52 = 40 Virginia provincials + 12 Mingo warriors under Tanacharison) and enemy_troop_strength (35 French) follow Wikipedia's more granular breakdown over the American Battlefield Trust's competing 87-vs-35 figures -- a real, unresolved disagreement flagged rather than picked apart further. enemy_casualties (31 = 10 killed + 21 captured) reflects 'most killed or captured' out of a 35-man party, consistent with contemporary accounts; a narrower reading (9-13 French dead only, no captures counted) also appears in some sources. Who actually killed Jumonville is separately disputed (musket fire during a summons reading vs. a tomahawk blow from Tanacharison after the shooting stopped) -- France used the ambiguity to accuse Washington of 'assassination,' a political charge that shaped the harsher terms of the Fort Necessity surrender five weeks later. Governor Dinwiddie's pre-authorization to 'kill & destroy' any French party encountered is context, not scored as political_constraint_flag here since it authorized rather than hampered Washington's conduct of the fight.

source_citation: Fred Anderson, 'Crucible of War' (2000); George Washington's after-action report, Founders Online (Washington Papers 02-01-02-0076-0002); National Park Service, 'Battle of Fort Necessity'
notes: own_troop_strength (393 = 293 Virginia Regiment + ~100 of Mackay's British regular Independent Company) and enemy_troop_strength (700 = ~600 French + ~100 Indian) follow NPS/Wikipedia's converging figures; the American Battlefield Trust's own page additionally gives an inconsistent '1,100 British / 369 captured' figure discarded here as a likely extraction artifact -- 369 captured stacked on 31 killed and 70 wounded would exceed the entire garrison, and more plausibly reflects the number who marched out under the surrender's honors-of-war terms (the garrison was permitted to withdraw with arms and colors, not taken prisoner). Loss driven by gunpowder degraded by rain, native allies withdrawing mid-battle, and a tactical misjudgment of how close the tree line sat to the fort -- but also by a genuine political/resource failure: Dinwiddie ordered the expedition without requesting funding from the Virginia House of Burgesses until after the fact, hence political_constraint_flag=true. Mackay held a royal commission that technically outranked Washington's provincial rank; no source checked resolves whether this created real friction over command, so 'Washington as sole commander' carries a minor asterisk.

source_citation: Henry P. Johnston, 'The Battle of Harlem Heights, September 16, 1776' (1897), described by Wikipedia as remaining 'the only detailed investigation of the battle'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Harlem Heights'
notes: Johnston's 1897 monograph is the de facto academic standard for this battle's casualty figures (30 American killed + 100 wounded = 130; 14 British killed + 157 wounded = 171) and no later source found revises it. opponent_general_id left blank: no single named British commander for this specific engagement was confirmed across sources checked. Washington personally devised the diversionary-ambush plan, committed Leitch's reinforcements, and called off the pursuit himself when British reserves approached, but did not personally lead the charge -- that fell to Knowlton and Leitch, both mortally wounded executing it. The day after the Kip's Bay rout, this is 'the first success of the war for the army directly under Washington's own command' and a real morale turning point.

source_citation: Mark Boatner, 'Encyclopedia of the American Revolution' (citing Fortescue's 'History of the British Army'); Rodney Atwood's corrected Hessian-casualty analysis; Henry P. Dawson
notes: enemy_casualties (267) corrects the commonly-repeated Fortescue/Boatner total of 313 (214 British + 99 Hessian): Atwood's analysis of the Hessian corps found only 53 of those 99 Hessian casualties actually occurred at White Plains, the rest bleeding in from the broader Oct 19-28 operations -- same 'prefer the corrected figure over an inflated aggregate' precedent used elsewhere in this dataset. own_casualties (233) is Dawson's whole-army figure (47 killed, 182 wounded, 4 missing); a narrower reading limited to just the engaged commands at Chatterton's Hill gives 217. Included despite the decisive local fight on Chatterton's Hill being run by subordinates (Spencer, then Haslet/McDougall) because Washington personally designed the fishhook defensive scheme and personally ordered the reinforcements to that position -- the same 'personally directed the overall army-level plan' standard already applied to Grant's Overland Campaign rows, distinct from the excluded Long Island/Fort Washington rows where Washington was not directing at all.

source_citation: David Hackett Fischer, 'Washington's Crossing' (2004), pp. 254-255, 391-396
notes: own_casualties (7) is 2 who died of exposure during the night march plus 5 wounded in the fighting -- Fischer states no American was killed in the assault itself. enemy_casualties (918) corrects a naive 22+83+800=905 sum: Fischer's own wording makes the 83 wounded a subset of the 896 captured ('896 captured, including the wounded'), giving 22 killed + 896 captured = 918. Washington personally led the advance element into contact with a Hessian outpost, riding at the front rather than directing from behind; undertaken by an army facing imminent mass enlistment expiration at year's end, the reason historians cite for accepting such a high-risk winter attack. Rall was mortally wounded in the fighting.

source_citation: David Hackett Fischer, 'Washington's Crossing' (2004), pp. 404, 412
notes: Casualty figures use Fischer's numbers (this dataset's designated source for the Trenton/Princeton campaign) but sit at the high end of a genuinely wide historiographic spread -- Stryker (1898) gives American losses of just 1 killed/6 wounded and Peckham gives 6 killed/10 wounded/1 deserted, an order of magnitude below Fischer's ~100, and Wikipedia itself declines to settle on one figure (citing a 7-100 American / 55-365 British range). Flagged rather than resolved, same 'document the disagreement' precedent used for Sekigahara and this general's own Monmouth row. Washington personally rode out to rally Hand's collapsing rear guard mid-battle, ordered the defensive earthworks along the creek, and chaired the war council that decided on the following night's march to Princeton -- direct, on-the-field command at the moment of crisis.

source_citation: David Hackett Fischer, 'Washington's Crossing' (2004); William S. Stryker, 'The Battles of Trenton and Princeton' (1898)
notes: own_troop_strength revised down from an initially-drafted 5,700 to Fischer's 4,500 -- the higher figure doesn't trace to Fischer or Stryker and appears to be a secondary-source rounding artifact. enemy_troop_strength (1,200) is the British force actually engaged, out of roughly 4,500 total in the wider Princeton garrison/theater. enemy_casualties (450) follows Stryker's explicit breakdown (100 killed, 70 wounded, 280 captured) over a commonly-repeated but uncited ~270 figure found in secondary aggregation. Washington personally led the counterattack after Hugh Mercer was mortally wounded and his brigade began to break, per the American Battlefield Trust's account of the decisive moment; Trenton, Assunpink Creek, and Princeton together form the best-documented cluster of personal, on-the-field command in Washington's career.

source_citation: Michael C. Harris and Gary Ecelbarger, 'The Numerical Strength of George Washington's Army During the 1777 Philadelphia Campaign', Journal of the American Revolution (Oct. 2021); Thomas J. McGuire, 'The Philadelphia Campaign, Vol. 1: Brandywine and the Fall of Philadelphia' (2006), p. 269
notes: own_troop_strength uses Harris & Ecelbarger's 2021 muster-record reconstruction (16,520, from a Sept 3, 1777 field return) over the older, still widely-repeated secondary estimate of ~14,600 -- same 'prefer the rigorously-sourced modern corrective' precedent already used for Caesar/Genghis/Hannibal/Subutai. enemy_casualties uses McGuire's direct quote of the British official return (93 killed, 488 wounded, 6 missing = 587) over contemporary American claims of 1,900-2,000, which McGuire attributes to unreliable distant observation. own_casualties (~1,300) is the commonly-cited round figure (Howe's report / Greene's independent estimate) but could not be pinned to a specific page in any source checked -- weaker sourcing than the other two figures in this row, contributing to the Low overall confidence. Washington personally misjudged how thoroughly the Brandywine fords were covered, letting the British flanking column cross undetected, then personally organized the fighting withdrawal once the flank collapsed. Fought amid the political pressure that coalesced that fall into the Conway Cabal -- political_constraint_flag=true, shared with Germantown and Whitemarsh below.

source_citation: Michael C. Harris and Gary Ecelbarger, Journal of the American Revolution (Oct. 2021); Thomas J. McGuire, 'The Philadelphia Campaign, Vol. 2' (2007), pp. 127-128; Jenkins, p. 142
notes: own_troop_strength uses the same Harris & Ecelbarger 2021 muster-record reconstruction as Brandywine (16,322, 'some 2,000 more than the estimate in a recent study') over the older ~11,000 figure (Ward) still common in popular accounts -- the largest such revision found anywhere in this dataset. Casualty figures are unusually well-pinned for an 18th-century battle: own_casualties (152 killed [Jenkins p.142] + 521 wounded + 438 captured [McGuire p.127] = 1,111) and enemy_casualties (71 killed + 448 wounded + 14 missing = 533, McGuire p.128, a direct quote) both confirmed with no revision needed. Washington personally devised the entire four-column double-envelopment night attack and made the on-field decision, over subordinates' objections, to keep attacking the British-held Chew House rather than bypass it -- a decision second-guessed by historians ever since. The Stephen/Wayne friendly-fire collision that unraveled the attack (Stephen, drunk during the battle, veered off course and was later court-martialed and cashiered) is an execution failure, not a deviation from Washington's own design. Same Conway-Cabal-adjacent political pressure window as Brandywine and Whitemarsh.

source_citation: Michael C. Harris and Gary Ecelbarger, Journal of the American Revolution (Oct. 2021); Thomas J. McGuire; Donald Jackson (ed.), citing Howe's official return, pp. 115, 308
notes: enemy_casualties (19 killed + 60 wounded + 33 missing = 112) is a direct quote of Howe's official return per Jackson; a separately-reported 238 British deserted is excluded from this field as both uncorroborated by a second source and outside the schema's killed/wounded/captured/missing definition of a casualty. own_casualties (~122) is assembled from several day-by-day sub-totals across Dec 5-8 (McGuire, Peckham, Martin) that overlap partially by unit and don't cleanly sum to one verified figure -- flagged Low confidence specifically for that reason, even though troop strength (from the same muster study used for Brandywine/Germantown) is comparatively solid. Fought during the same congressional-pressure/collapsing-supply-system window as Brandywine and Germantown (Quartermaster General Mifflin resigned Oct 8, 1777; Washington warned Congress on Dec 23 that 'this Army might dissolve' without fixes) -- political_constraint_flag=true for the same reason. Washington personally built the entrenched position and made the defensive decision not to sally out; a minor, skirmish-level action relative to the rest of this roster (casualties over an order of magnitude below Brandywine's or Germantown's) but a genuine personal command with quantifiable figures on both sides, and one that directly enabled the safe march to Valley Forge.

source_citation: Mark Edward Lender and Garry Wheeler Stone, 'Fatal Sunday: George Washington, the Monmouth Campaign, and the Politics of Battle' (2016); Gen. Henry Clinton's official report
notes: Personal command applies only to the second half of this battle -- Charles Lee independently commanded roughly a third of the army (4,500-5,000 men) in the opening vanguard action and its collapsing retreat before Washington rode up, relieved him of command on the spot, and personally reorganized the three-line defense that held for the rest of the day (Lee was later court-martialed for disobeying orders, misbehavior in retreating, and disrespect toward the commander-in-chief). own_casualties uses Lender & Stone's modern reconstruction ('could have exceeded 500') over the official 1778 report's 370, same 'prefer the rigorous modern corrective' precedent used elsewhere in this dataset; enemy_casualties uses Clinton's own official report (358) over the Monmouth County Historical Association's modern estimate of 1,134, since the Association is a local historical society rather than a named academic military historian -- flagged as the widest, and only inverted-direction, casualty disagreement in this dataset, most likely reflecting different conventions for counting heat-stroke deaths and desertions rather than a genuine battlefield dispute. enemy_troop_strength (5,400) is the British force actually engaged, out of a much larger theater force (up to ~21,000) mostly not committed to the fight.

source_citation: American Battlefield Trust, 'Siege of Yorktown'; Wikipedia 'Siege of Yorktown' (combined allied troop figures); Comte de Rochambeau's memoirs via American Revolution Institute (command-protocol quote)
notes: own_troop_strength (19,800) and own_casualties (643 = 389 American [88 killed, 301 wounded] + 254 French [60 killed, 194 wounded]) combine both national contingents into one field under Washington's protocol-supreme command -- the same 'combine multi-force figures, document it' treatment already used for Alesia and Zhukov's Vistula-Oder Offensive elsewhere in this dataset. Louis XVI had ordered Rochambeau to treat Washington as his superior officer, confirmed directly by Rochambeau's own memoir account of the Oct 19 surrender ceremony ('the French army being only an auxiliary on this continent, it devolved on the American General to tend him his orders'). The French casualty component (254) is the weakest-sourced figure in this entire roster -- it appears consistently across several tertiary web sources but could not be traced to a named academic historian (Mackesy, Dull, Ketchum) in the research done for this row; flagged explicitly rather than presented as equally solid as the American figure, and source_confidence is set Low specifically because of it. Operationally, command stayed split by nationality even under Washington's overall authority -- the climactic Oct 14 night assault saw American light infantry under Hamilton storm Redoubt No. 10 while French regulars under Deux-Ponts stormed Redoubt No. 9, neither personally led by Washington -- a real authority/formal-hierarchy split similar in shape to (though mirrored from) Subutai's Mohi row elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Jac Weller, Wellington in India (1972); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflict; Wikipedia 'Battle of Assaye'
notes: Early-career command under the Wellesley name, six years before the Peninsular War -- included as a scope call (see generals.csv) matching Napoleon's Montenotte precedent for a general's first independent command. enemy_troop_strength is a soft mid-estimate; irregular-cavalry counts vary roughly 2-4x across sources depending what's included. own_troop_strength includes ~2,000 unarmed camp followers alongside ~4,500 actual combat troops. opponent_general_id is Anthony Pohlmann, the European mercenary who trained and tactically led the Maratha regular infantry; Scindia and Bhonsle held nominal princely command.

source_citation: Jac Weller, Wellington in India (1972); Wikipedia 'Battle of Argaon'
notes: enemy_casualties is genuinely disputed across sources: the more commonly cited figure is ~5,000 killed, but an alternate breakdown gives closer to 2,000 killed+wounded combined -- flagged, not resolved. opponent_general_id left blank: after Assaye scattered Pohlmann's brigades, no single Maratha field commander is identifiable across sources. Effectively ended organized Maratha field resistance within weeks.

source_citation: William Napier, History of the War in the Peninsula, Vol. I; Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. I; Wikipedia 'Battle of Roliça'
notes: Wellesley's first Peninsular battle -- a small rearguard action (Delaborde withdrew in reasonably good order) that opened the six-year campaign, the parallel to Washington's Jumonville Glen in this dataset. political_constraint_flag=true: government seniority rules meant Wellesley knew more senior generals were already en route to supersede him, a real constraint on how far he could exploit the win.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. I; William Napier, History of the War in the Peninsula, Vol. I; Wikipedia 'Battle of Vimeiro'
notes: Command-attribution edge case: Lt. Gen. Sir Harry Burrard arrived offshore the day before and technically outranked Wellesley, but stayed aboard ship and let him fight the battle as already deployed, then blocked the pursuit afterward -- Wellesley personally directed the battle itself (included per this dataset's personal-command bar) but was not free to exploit the win, hence political_constraint_flag=true. Led directly to the French evacuation of Portugal via the Convention of Cintra.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. II; William Napier, History of the War in the Peninsula, Vol. II; Wikipedia 'Battle of Talavera'
notes: own figures are Wellesley's British force only (20,641), not combined with General Cuesta's ~34,800 Spanish troops -- no source found any formal subordination of Cuesta to Wellesley (unlike Washington's Yorktown/Rochambeau), and the Spanish force was only lightly engaged, so combining would credit troops Wellesley didn't direct. Held the field against repeated French assaults, but a supply crisis (partly caused by Spanish logistical failures) forced a retreat to Portugal days later -- same tactical-win-no-strategic-payoff pattern as Napoleon's Borodino. opponent_general_id is Marshal Victor, who planned and led the main French assaults; Joseph Bonaparte held nominal supreme command. source_confidence=Low: Oman himself calls Cuesta's claimed 1,201 Spanish casualties implausibly high given how lightly his force fought.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. III; Wikipedia 'Battle of Bussaco'
notes: Deliberately fought as a delaying/bleeding action ahead of the planned withdrawal to the prepared Lines of Torres Vedras -- abandoning the ridge days later was the intended plan, not a failure to hold ground.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. IV; Wikipedia 'Battle of Fuentes de Oñoro'
notes: Repelled Masséna's relief attempt on besieged Almeida -- Wellington himself called it a near-run thing ('If Boney had been there, we should have been beat'). objective_secured=true for the stated battle objective (relief repelled), though the Almeida garrison itself slipped through the lines and escaped two nights later, undercutting the fuller campaign goal.

source_citation: Ian Fletcher, Vauban's Nightmare: The Siege and Storming of Ciudad Rodrigo (Osprey Campaign series); Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. V; Wikipedia 'Siege of Ciudad Rodrigo (1812)'
notes: Opened the northern invasion gateway into Spain. enemy_casualties reflects that essentially the whole small garrison was killed, wounded, or captured. opponent_general_id is the fortress governor, Jean Leonard Barrié.

source_citation: Ian Fletcher, Badajoz 1812: Wellington's Bloodiest Siege (Osprey Campaign series); Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. V; Wikipedia 'Siege of Badajoz (1812)'
notes: Own casualties in the final storming alone rival the entire garrison's losses -- Wellington reportedly wept at the sight of the breaches afterward. The fortress was secured but at an appalling, historically infamous cost, the same nominal-win/gutted-force pattern as Napoleon's Wagram row.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. V; Charles Esdaile, The Peninsular War: A New History; Wikipedia 'Battle of Salamanca'
notes: Marmont's army shattered in an afternoon -- Jomini's oft-quoted line is that Wellington 'defeated an army of 40,000 men in 40 minutes.' opponent_general_id is Marmont, whose dispositions and plan the battle is named for, even though he was wounded early and Bertrand Clauzel took over the collapsing command mid-battle -- same credit-the-plan's-author convention as Grant's Shiloh row naming Albert Sidney Johnston.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VI; Wikipedia 'Siege of Burgos'
notes: Widely regarded as Wellington's clearest field failure -- included for the same reason Napoleon's Leipzig and Washington's Brandywine/Germantown are included, an honest record rather than a highlight reel. own_troop_strength is the whole covering army; the actual assault parties thrown at the walls were a small fraction of this. political_constraint_flag=true: the siege train was inadequate (five heavy guns, three mortars, under 3,000 rounds), a documented logistical/political failure traceable to inadequate support from Lisbon/London, unlike his other 1812 sieges.

source_citation: Charles Esdaile, The Peninsular War: A New History; Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VI; Wikipedia 'Battle of Vitoria'
notes: Unlike Talavera, own_troop_strength combines the full multinational Allied total (British/Portuguese/Spanish): by 1813 Spanish divisions (Longa, Morillo) were genuinely integrated into Wellington's single order of battle and personally directed by him, unlike Cuesta's separate 1809 command. Joseph Bonaparte's army and baggage train collapsed; effectively ended French rule in Spain. own_troop_strength has a real spread across sources -- a simpler, commonly-cited '75,000' figure appears alongside the more granular 81,000-90,000 breakdown used here.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VI; Wikipedia 'Battle of Sorauren'
notes: Narrowed from the sprawling week-long 'Battle of the Pyrenees' (25 Jul-2 Aug) to Sorauren specifically, the one action within it Wellington personally rode to and commanded -- several simultaneous passes in the wider campaign were fought by subordinates (Picton, Byng, Cole) without him present, the same personal-command bar that excludes Auerstedt from Napoleon's Jena row. Halted Soult's offensive to relieve San Sebastián/Pamplona, forcing a French retreat by 2 August.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Nivelle'
notes: Breached Soult's fortified Bidasoa-Nivelle defensive line, opening the invasion of France itself. Figures used are the 'engaged' subset of each side's larger theatre-wide totals (90,000/50,000), since Soult's line was thinly spread and only part of each army was actually committed to this action.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Nive'
notes: A hard-fought, multi-day defensive success against repeated French counterattacks near Bayonne, consolidating the Allied position without a decisive breakthrough of its own -- unlike the Nivelle and Orthez rows bracketing it in time.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Orthez'
notes: Broke Soult's defensive line inside France, forcing a retreat toward Toulouse.

source_citation: Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, Vol. VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Toulouse (1814)'
notes: A 'hollow triumph' per multiple historians: Soult's army withdrew intact rather than being destroyed, and unknown to either commander at the time, Napoleon had already abdicated three days earlier, making the battle strategically moot -- same tactical-win-no-strategic-payoff treatment as Napoleon's Borodino and this general's own Talavera row. enemy_casualties is genuinely disputed (a 2,000-3,236 range across sources); the low end of that range is used here, flagged rather than resolved.

source_citation: David Chandler, Waterloo: The Hundred Days; Wikipedia 'Battle of Quatre Bras'
notes: Held the crossroads at dusk and denied Ney the position, allowing an orderly, deliberate withdrawal the next day to link up with Blücher's line at Waterloo, not a forced retreat. political_constraint_flag=true: Wellington was famously caught off guard by Napoleon's opening moves while at the Duchess of Richmond's ball in Brussels, and coalition coordination with the Prussians was a live constraint through the whole campaign.

source_citation: David Chandler, Waterloo: The Hundred Days; Jac Weller, Wellington at Waterloo; Wikipedia 'Battle of Waterloo'
notes: own_troop_strength/own_casualties are Wellington's Anglo-allied army only, deliberately not combined with Blücher's Prussians (~45,000 troops, ~8,000 casualties) -- unlike Washington's Yorktown or Zhukov's Vistula-Oder, no protocol-supreme-command relationship existed between the two coalition partners (nothing like Louis XVI's explicit subordination order at Yorktown), so each general's row reports only the force he personally commanded. enemy_troop_strength/enemy_casualties are set to match napoleon-waterloo-1815's own_troop_strength/own_casualties exactly (72,000 / 34,500) for cross-dataset consistency; that existing row's enemy_troop_strength/enemy_casualties (113,000 / 23,500) are the combined Anglo+Prussian totals, a documented, intentional asymmetry between the two generals' rows for the same battle. resource_backing_tier=3, higher than Napoleon's 1 on his own row, reflecting Wellington's backing by the full British Treasury/coalition subsidy system even though this was still a hastily-scratch, mixed-quality multinational army.

source_citation: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; Sears, To the Gates of Richmond (1992)
notes: Lee's first battle as army commander (he took over the Army of Northern Virginia June 1, 1862 after Johnston was wounded at Seven Pines) and the only clean tactical victory of the Seven Days -- a massed evening assault finally broke Fitz John Porter's V Corps line along Boatswain's Swamp, forcing Porter's night withdrawal across the Chickahominy and setting up McClellan's full retreat toward the James. opponent_general_id is Fitz John Porter, the actual field commander that day; McClellan remained at his headquarters south of the river and was not present on the battlefield. Coded Strategic rather than Rout: Porter's corps was pushed off the field but withdrew in reasonably good order, not destroyed. The day before (Battle of Beaver Dam Creek/Mechanicsville, June 26) is excluded from this roster -- Lee's frontal assaults there were repulsed with heavy Confederate casualties and Porter's overnight withdrawal was his own pre-planned move to a stronger line, not a result Lee's attack achieved, so it does not clear this dataset's no-fabricated-strategic-credit standard the way Gaines's Mill does the next day.

source_citation: Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts; Sears, To the Gates of Richmond (1992)
notes: The last and costliest of the Seven Days: repeated, poorly coordinated frontal assaults against a massed Union artillery position on the high ground were repulsed with roughly double the Confederate casualties of the defenders -- D.H. Hill's own verdict ('It was not war, it was murder') is the standard historian summary. Coded a clean Loss/objective_secured=false on the tactical letter of the battle, distinct from the Seven Days campaign's overall strategic outcome (McClellan continued his already-underway withdrawal to Harrison's Landing afterward, but that was his own prior decision, not a result Lee's attack here achieved -- the same distinction drawn for Beaver Dam Creek in the Gaines's Mill row's notes). opponent_general_id is McClellan, who was personally present and directing the defense here, unlike Gaines's Mill the previous day.

source_citation: Hennessy, Return to Bull Run (1993); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Lee's decisive Second Manassas campaign victory: Jackson's wing held Pope's army fixed against an unfinished railroad cut for two days while Longstreet's wing marched up undetected and delivered a massive flank assault on August 30, driving Pope's army back to the Washington defenses in a rout comparable to First Bull Run the year before. Coded Rout despite Pope's retreat being conducted in reasonable order (unlike First Bull Run's panic) because the army was driven from the field and effectively destroyed as an independent fighting force -- it was dissolved into the Army of the Potomac within days and Pope was relieved. own/enemy strength and casualty figures carry a real cross-source spread: the National Park Service's battle-only tally (13,830 Union / 8,350 Confederate) versus Eicher's full Northern Virginia campaign totals, which fold in Cedar Mountain and Chantilly (16,054 Union / 9,197 Confederate) -- the battle-scoped figures used here (14,462 / 7,298) split the difference and are the figures most secondary sources settle on for the battle itself; source_confidence downgraded to Medium for that spread. Lee himself later regretted not destroying Pope's army outright, per Hennessy.

source_citation: Sears, Landscape Turned Red (1983); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: The bloodiest single day of the war. Neither army broke on the field itself on September 17 -- Lee held his ground through September 18 before withdrawing back across the Potomac unmolested the night of the 18th-19th, which is why some tallies label the battle tactically inconclusive. It is coded Loss rather than Draw here because Lee's own stated campaign objective (win a battle on Northern soil to encourage Maryland secessionists, British/French recognition, and Northern Peace Democrats ahead of the 1862 midterms -- hence political_constraint_flag=true) was not achieved, the invasion ended in full withdrawal from Maryland, and Lincoln used the outcome as the occasion to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later; Wikipedia's own extensively-discussed infobox result field likewise settles on 'Union victory.' own_troop_strength/enemy_troop_strength here use present-for-duty totals (Sears: ~38,000 Confederate, ~75,000-87,000 Union present, not all engaged) rather than the narrower 'engaged' figures (30,646 / 53,632) some infoboxes report, matching the engaged-vs-present distinction already used for Champion Hill/Vicksburg in Grant's roster; casualty figures (12,410 Union, 10,316 Confederate) agree closely across Sears, NPS, and Clodfelter, but confidence is kept at Medium for the strength-figure spread.

source_citation: O'Reilly, The Fredericksburg Campaign (2003); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: A one-sided defensive win: repeated Union frontal assaults against the sunken road at Marye's Heights were repulsed with more than double Lee's own casualties, and Burnside withdrew his army back across the Rappahannock two days later. Coded Strategic rather than Rout -- the Army of the Potomac was badly bloodied and demoralized but retreated intact, not destroyed as a fighting force, the same distinction used for Fort Donelson-level Routs elsewhere in this dataset not applying here. Strength and casualty figures agree closely across O'Reilly, NPS, and Clodfelter.

source_citation: Sears, Chancellorsville (1996); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Historians' standard pick for Lee's tactical masterpiece: outnumbered better than 2-to-1, he split his army twice, sending Jackson on a march around Hooker's exposed right flank for a collapsing rout that forced Hooker's full withdrawal back across the Rappahannock. Coded decisiveness=Pyrrhic despite objective_secured=true because Confederate casualties (12,764, roughly 21% of the force engaged) ran proportionally higher than Union losses (17,287 of a much larger army, roughly 13%), and Stonewall Jackson was mortally wounded by his own pickets during the flank march and died eight days later -- Lee's own reported reaction ('He has lost his left arm, but I have lost my right') and the loss of his most effective corps commander for the rest of the war are the standard reasons historians treat this as a win that gutted the force, the same Pyrrhic pattern already used for Napoleon's Borodino in this dataset. own_troop_strength/own_casualties and enemy figures here use the full Chancellorsville campaign totals (Hooker's 133,868 present-for-duty, 17,287 campaign casualties) rather than the narrower main-battle-only tallies (~106,000 / 12,145) some infobox variants report, following the same 'conventionally reported for the whole named battle' convention used for Grant's Shiloh row; source_confidence downgraded to Medium for that campaign-vs-battle-only spread.

source_citation: Busey & Martin, Regimental Losses in the American Civil War (2005 rev.); Sears, Gettysburg (2003)
notes: Lee's greatest defeat and the high-water mark of the Confederacy: three days of escalating attacks culminated in Pickett's Charge against the Union center on July 3, repulsed with catastrophic losses, forcing a full retreat back into Virginia and ending the second and last Confederate invasion of the North. political_constraint_flag=true reflects the invasion's own political rationale (relieve Virginia's exhausted farmland, win a battle on Northern soil to strengthen Copperhead peace sentiment and European recognition prospects) -- the same category of political motivation flagged on the Antietam row. Confederate casualties are this row's one genuinely disputed figure: infobox ranges run 23,000-28,000 depending on source; the Busey & Martin regimental-return-based figure (23,231) used here is the tally most modern historians (including Sears) treat as the best-supported academic estimate, rather than the higher contemporary Confederate self-reports -- source_confidence downgraded to Low for this spread, the same treatment given other battles in this dataset with a comparably wide casualty-estimate range (e.g. Borodino). Not coded Rout: the Army of Northern Virginia retreated across the Potomac in fighting order over the following week and remained an intact, effective fighting force for nearly two more years, unlike the Rout-level collapses at Appomattox or Waterloo elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Rhea, The Battle of the Wilderness (1994); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of the existing grant-wilderness-1864 row (own/enemy strength and casualty figures swapped so both rows agree on the same battle), the first of seven Lee rows that overlap Grant's roster -- same treatment as the Hannibal/Scipio Zama pair and the Napoleon/Wellington Waterloo pair elsewhere in this dataset. Recorded as a Draw on the same 'inconclusive, neither army broke' standard as Grant's row: Lee checked Grant's advance through the dense terrain and inflicted disproportionate casualties, but Grant's decision to continue the march south rather than withdraw (unlike every prior Union commander in Virginia after a bloody check) meant Lee's actual strategic objective -- stopping the 1864 Overland Campaign -- was not secured, hence objective_secured=false on this row too. political_constraint_flag=true reflects Davis's and the Confederate government's mounting pressure to defend Richmond directly rather than maneuver freely, a constraint that only tightens through the rest of Lee's roster below -- a different source of political pressure than Grant's own election-cycle flag on the mirrored row, noted here since the two flags track different constraints despite describing the same battles.

source_citation: Rhea, The Battle of Spotsylvania Court House (1997); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-spotsylvania-1864; same Low source_confidence as that row for the same reason (Wikipedia's 108,000-115,400 Union / 52,000-63,000 Confederate range versus ABT's 152,000 / 100,000 total-effective-strength figures, a 40,000+ spread most likely explained by troops actually engaged at Spotsylvania versus total army strength). Two weeks of fighting, including the 'Bloody Angle' at the Mule Shoe salient, ended with Lee's line intact but Grant again sidestepping south rather than withdrawing -- Draw/objective_secured=false on the same standard as the Wilderness row.

source_citation: Rhea, Cold Harbor (2002); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-cold-harbor-1864, Grant's clearest Loss of the war and correspondingly Lee's clearest defensive Win of the Overland Campaign: the entrenched Confederate line repulsed the June 3 frontal assault at roughly a 1-to-2.4 casualty ratio in Lee's favor. Coded Strategic rather than Rout, matching Grant's own row -- the Army of the Potomac was checked and badly bloodied but not destroyed, and within days maneuvered south across the James toward Petersburg anyway, so the win did not end the campaign despite its lopsided cost. Same Low source_confidence as Grant's row for the same Wikipedia-vs-ABT troop-strength spread; enemy_casualties (12,738) reflects Grant's own_casualties figure which Gordon Rhea has argued is more defensible than the popular '7,000-in-20-minutes' narrative for June 3 alone.

source_citation: Trudeau, The Last Citadel (1991); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-crater-1864. After a mine detonation blew a gap in the Confederate lines, the follow-up Union assault (a division that Burnside's own preferred, specially-trained replacement had been pulled from at the last minute by Meade) collapsed into the resulting crater and was destroyed there by a counterattack led on the ground by William Mahone, under Lee's overall command of the Petersburg defenses -- coded Rout, unlike the Loss-side decisiveness field elsewhere in this roster, because the opposing Union assault force was effectively destroyed in place (roughly 44% casualties among the divisions actually sent into the crater). This is the first of this roster's three siege-phase rows where Lee, not a subordinate, is the correct opponent_general_id despite a subordinate (Mahone here, A.P. Hill at Globe Tavern) leading the actual counterattack on the ground -- same 'personally supreme-commanded' standard Grant's own Wilderness/Spotsylvania rows use for the Grant/Meade split. The Second Battle of Petersburg (June 15-18, 1864), by contrast, is excluded from this roster entirely: per Grant's own row for that battle, the thin defending garrison was commanded solely by P.G.T. Beauregard, with Lee's army arriving from the Overland Campaign only as the assaults were already ending -- a genuinely different case from the Crater/Globe Tavern/Third Petersburg rows below, and excluded under the same subordinate-command bar used to exclude battles from Grant's, Genghis Khan's, Saladin's, and Frederick's rosters elsewhere in this dataset, not an oversight.

source_citation: Trudeau, The Last Citadel (1991); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-globe-tavern-1864. Confederate counterattacks (led by A.P. Hill on the ground, under Lee's overall command of the siege lines, the same overall-vs-tactical-command split as the Crater row above) failed to retake the Weldon Railroad, one of Petersburg's last open supply lines, despite inflicting more than double the Union casualties -- the railroad stayed permanently cut for the rest of the siege, a genuine strategic loss for Lee's supply situation regardless of the lopsided casualty count in his favor, hence Loss/objective_secured=false rather than a casualty-ratio-based Win.

source_citation: Trudeau, The Last Citadel (1991); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-third-petersburg-1865. Union forces finally broke through Lee's badly thinned defensive lines, killing Lee's corps commander A.P. Hill and forcing the evacuation of Petersburg and Richmond that night, triggering the week-long retreat that ended at Appomattox. political_constraint_flag=true here, unlike the false flag on Grant's mirrored row -- Grant's flag tracked the 1864 US election cycle, which had already resolved by this point, but Jefferson Davis's standing order to hold the Confederate capital at essentially any cost remained in force right up until this breakthrough itself forced the evacuation, a different and longer-lived political constraint than Grant's, the same kind of documented asymmetry between two generals' rows for the same battle as the Waterloo/Wellington pair elsewhere in this dataset. Not coded Rout, matching Grant's own reasoning for this row: the Army of Northern Virginia's line was broken here, but the army itself retreated in some order toward Appomattox rather than disintegrating on this specific field.

source_citation: Freeman, R. E. Lee: A Biography (1934); Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts
notes: Mirror of grant-appomattox-1865, the last battle of Lee's roster: surrounded, out of supplies, and with his army reduced to a fraction of its Overland Campaign strength through desertion, combat losses, and the destruction of his supply trains at Sailor's Creek days earlier, Lee fought a brief final skirmish and then surrendered -- coded Loss/Rout on the same 'this general's own army was the one that broke' standard already used for Napoleon's Waterloo and Hannibal's Zama rows elsewhere in this dataset. enemy_casualties (164) is Grant's own_casualties figure from that mirrored row; own_casualties (26,500) combines the day's light combat losses with the roughly 26,000 troops surrendered, the same 'surrendered-army-as-casualties' convention used for Vicksburg, Fort Donelson, and Grant's own version of this row. political_constraint_flag=false, a change from every row since the Wilderness: by this point the Confederate government had already fled Richmond and Davis's standing hold-the-capital order (flagged on the Third Petersburg row above) no longer bound Lee -- the decision to surrender rather than disperse the army for guerrilla warfare (which some subordinates urged) was Lee's own military and moral judgment, not a political constraint imposed on him.
